newsitem.title: TAIWAN: China curbs Taiwan officials' HK visits -report.
newsitem.headline: China curbs Taiwan officials' HK visits -report.

text.p: Hong Kong, under pressure from China, has rejected several visa applications from Taiwan officials to visit the British colony, Taiwan's official Central News Agency reported on Monday.

"Communist China recently has pressured the Hong Kong and British governments to restrict visits by Taiwan officials to Hong Hong," the agency quoted an unnamed official at the cabinet's Mainland Affairs Council as saying.

Hong Kong, which reverts to China's rule on July 1 next year, has rejected visa applications from Yen Chin-feng, a minister without portfolio, and Wang Nung-chang, a director of the ruling Nationalist Party, the official said.
The British colony also rejected several visa applications from other senior Taiwan officials, the official said.
"Communist China's unreasonable move under the table to restrict (such visits) will not help Hong Kong's freedom, prosperity and peaceful handover," the council official said.
If officials from Taiwan and Hong Kong could not exchange visits after the 1997 handover, normal Taiwan-Hong Kong economic communications could not be maintained, the official added.

The sides have signed aviation accords that will allow air links between Taiwan and post-transition Hong Kong, but similar pacts for shipping and many other economic links remain to be negotiated -- fuelling growing uncertainty for investors.
Hong Kong's return to China is seen by some as a step towards the reunification of Taiwan and China, which were separated by a civil war in 1949 and remain estranged officially.
Many analysts say direct economic links between Taiwan and a Beijing-ruled Hong Kong will enable Beijing to increase pressure on Taipei to allow direct links with other parts of China.
Taiwan has banned all direct contact with China since 1949 but has tolerated business, social and cultural links across the Taiwan strait since a bilateral thaw began in the late 1980s.
Still, Taipei requires that all trade with and investment in China must be routed through a third region, chiefly Hong Kong.
The Taipei and Beijing governments both say they want reunification, but under very different terms.

China says that under Beijing's rule, Taiwan could keep its political and social structures under the "one country, two systems" model pioneered for Hong Kong. Taipei counters that only adoption by China of broad democratic reforms like Taiwan's own will make reunification viable.
